output.title: Present tense verbs for describing your daily work routine
output.body:
When describing your daily work routine in English, you will primarily use the present simple tense. This tense is used for habits, regular actions, and facts. In a professional context, it helps you describe your responsibilities and typical workday clearly.

Verb forms for daily routines

For most verbs, the base form remains the same for all subjects, except for the third person singular (he/she/it), where you add an -s or -es ending.

I start work at 9:00.

He starts work at 9:00.

We finish work at 6:00.

They finish work at 6:00.

Common verbs for work routines:

start / begin: I start work at 8:30.

finish / end: We finish work at 5:30.

check: I check my emails every morning.

reply / answer: She replies to customers.

call / phone: He calls his team every Monday.

meet: We meet with clients on Tuesdays.

organise / organize: She organises the weekly meetings.

write: I write reports every Friday.

read: He reads the news every morning.


Adverbs of frequency

To make your descriptions more precise, use adverbs of frequency. These usually go before the main verb.

I always start work at 8:30.

We usually finish work at 6:00.

She often checks her emails.

He never works on weekends.


Common time expressions

When describing a routine, we often use time expressions at the end of the sentence.

I check my emails every morning.

We meet with clients on Tuesdays.

He writes reports every Friday.

I start work at 8:30.

We finish work at 6:00.


Practice

Try to describe your own work day using the verbs and structures above. Remember to use the -s ending for he/she/it.

Example:

I start work at 9:00. I check my emails and then I start my daily tasks. I usually have lunch at 12:30. In the afternoon, I meet with my team. I finish work at 6:00.

My colleague starts work at 9:30. She checks her emails and then she starts her daily tasks. She usually has lunch at 1:00. In the afternoon, she meets with her team. She finishes work at 6:30.

output.title: Explaining a project delay to a manager

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Hi, Sarah. Do you have a moment? I wanted to check in on the status of the new marketing campaign. Is everything on track for the launch next week?

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: Actually, I’m afraid I have some news. We’re going to need to push back the launch date.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Oh? That’s not what I expected to hear. What’s the reason for the delay?

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: Well, we’ve run into a bit of a snag with the website design. The external agency we hired is behind schedule, and they haven't finished the mobile-responsive layout yet.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: I see. How much of a delay are we talking about? A few days or a few weeks?

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: I think we’ll need at least two weeks. We want to make sure the user experience is seamless before we go live. If we launch now, it could hurt our brand image.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: I understand. Quality is important. Have you discussed this with the stakeholders?

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: Yes, I’ve already briefed the department heads. They’re aware of the situation and agree that a short delay is better than a buggy launch.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Alright. What’s the plan to get us back on track as quickly as possible?

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: I’ve scheduled a daily check-in with the agency’s project manager starting tomorrow. I’ll also be overseeing the final QA testing personally to ensure there are no further hold-ups.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Thanks for being proactive about this, Sarah. Keep me updated on the progress. I’ll let the executive team know.

output.title: Polite Requests in the Workplace: Modal Verbs
output.body:
When making requests in a professional environment, the choice of modal verb significantly impacts the level of politeness and formality. In English, direct requests can sometimes sound demanding or rude, so modal verbs are essential for softening your tone.

1. Can you / Could you

“Can you” is common and appropriate for colleagues you know well or for routine tasks. However, “Could you” is the standard for professional requests as it sounds more polite and less demanding.

• Can you send me the agenda for tomorrow’s meeting?
• Could you please let me know when the report is finished?

2. May I / Could I

Use “May I” or “Could I” when asking for permission to do something. This is more formal than “Can I.”

• May I borrow your stapler for a moment?
• Could I leave a few minutes early today?

3. Would you mind / Would it be possible

These structures are highly polite and are ideal for making requests that might inconvenience the other person. They are often followed by a gerund (verb + -ing).

• Would you mind checking this draft for me?
• Would it be possible to reschedule our call to Friday?

4. Would you be able to / Would you be willing to

These are useful when you are unsure if the other person has the time or desire to help.

• Would you be able to take a look at this proposal?
• Would you be willing to lead the presentation next week?

Key Tips:

• Add “please” to any request to increase politeness.
• Use “I was wondering if you could...” to make a request sound even softer and less direct.
• Avoid using “I want” or “I need” directly (e.g., “I need you to do this”), as these can sound aggressive. Instead, use “I would appreciate it if you could...”

output.title: Disagreeing Diplomatically in a Business Context

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: I think we should consider launching the new product line in the UK market as soon as possible. The sooner we start, the sooner we can establish a foothold.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.text: I see your point, Sarah, and I agree that we need to be proactive. However, I'm not sure that launching right now is the best move.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: Why do you say that? We've already done the market research.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.text: Well, while the research is solid, I'm concerned about our current production capacity. If we launch now, we might struggle to keep up with demand, which could hurt our reputation.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: That's a valid concern. But wouldn't it be better to risk a slow start than to delay the launch indefinitely?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.text: I don't think it's an either-or situation. Perhaps we could consider a phased rollout? We could launch in a few key cities first to test the waters before going nationwide.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.text: That's an interesting idea. It would allow us to manage our resources more effectively while still making progress.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.text: Exactly. It's a way to mitigate the risks while still moving forward with the launch.

body.notes: This dialogue demonstrates how to disagree politely by acknowledging the other person's point before presenting a counter-argument. Key phrases include 'I see your point,' 'I'm not sure that... is the best move,' and 'That's a valid concern.'

output.title: Conditional Sentences for Hypothetical Business Scenarios
output.body:
In a professional context, conditional sentences are essential for discussing possibilities, risks, and hypothetical outcomes. They allow you to explore different scenarios without committing to a specific action. There are three main types of conditionals used in business, each serving a distinct purpose.

1. The First Conditional (Real Possibilities)

We use the first conditional to talk about real possibilities in the future. It describes a situation that is likely to happen if a specific condition is met. 

Structure: If + present simple, will + infinitive.

Example: If we sign the contract by Friday, we will start the project next month.

Note: You can also use modal verbs like 'can', 'may', or 'might' instead of 'will' to express varying degrees of certainty.

Example: If the market trends continue, we might increase our market share by 5%.

2. The Second Conditional (Hypothetical Scenarios)

We use the second conditional to talk about imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future. It is often used for brainstorming, brainstorming, or discussing 'what if' scenarios.

Structure: If + past simple, would + infinitive.

Example: If we had a larger marketing budget, we would hire more specialists.

Note: In formal writing, 'were' is preferred over 'was' for the verb 'to be' in the if-clause.

Example: If the CEO were here, she would approve the proposal immediately.

3. The Third Conditional (Past Regrets and Analysis)

We use the third conditional to talk about the past. It describes a situation that did not happen and explores the hypothetical consequences of that past event. This is frequently used in post-project reviews or when analyzing past mistakes.

Structure: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

Example: If we had invested earlier, we would have secured a better price.

4. Mixed Conditionals

Sometimes, the condition and the result occur in different time frames. The most common mixed conditional combines a past condition with a present result.

Structure: If + past perfect, would + infinitive.

Example: If we had hired the right consultant last year, our current situation would be much better.

Key Vocabulary for Business Conditionals:

- Provided that / Providing that (more formal than 'if'): If we provide the training, they will be able to use the software.
- As long as / So long as: We will support the project as long as we meet our quarterly targets.
- Unless (if not): Unless we increase production, we will lose market share.

Practice Tip:
When discussing strategy, try to move from the first conditional (discussing likely outcomes) to the second conditional (exploring alternative strategies) to show a range of possibilities.

- Unless (if not): Unless we increase production, we will lose market share.

Practice Tip:
When discussing strategy, try to move from the first conditional (discussing likely outcomes) to the second conditional (exploring alternative strategies) to show a range of possibilities."
}

output.title: Formal Complaint: Late Delivery of Goods

body.instructions:
You are a purchasing manager for a medium-sized manufacturing company. You ordered a large shipment of industrial components from a supplier, 'Global Parts Inc.', which was due to arrive last Friday. The shipment has not arrived, and you have received no communication regarding a delay. Write a formal letter of complaint to the supplier. In your letter, you should:

- State clearly what the problem is and refer to your original order.

- Explain the negative impact the delay is having on your production schedule.

- Request an immediate update on the status of the shipment.

- State what action you expect the supplier to take to rectify the situation.

- Maintain a professional and firm tone throughout.
